summary: Provides a framework for operating and managing Layer 3 Virtual Private Networks. It describes the significant technical issues for management solutions but leaves specific approaches, models and protocols out of scope. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A private tunnel through a shared network needs people to watch over it. This memo is a checklist of what to think about when managing those tunnels.

subtitle: What operators need to know about managing Layer 3 virtual private networks.

tldr.problem: Operating and managing Layer 3 Virtual Private Networks requires balancing the needs of customers and service providers across complex shared infrastructure. The technical issues are significant but have not been systematized.
tldr.mechanism: This document outlines a management framework covering two main layers: customer service management (what customers see and control) and provider network management (how providers maintain the infrastructure). It describes the functions, information models, and architecture needed at each layer.
tldr.outcome: The framework provides a foundation for designing management solutions without specifying particular approaches, protocols, or products. It is informational and reflects the state of understanding in 2005.

today: RFC 4176 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It remains an important reference for understanding the architecture of VPN management systems. Vendors and service providers continue to use similar frameworks when designing management platforms, though many now support additional protocols beyond SNMP.

sections.title: Layer 3 Virtual Private Networks
sections.content:
A Layer 3 Virtual Private Network (L3VPN) is a way to connect multiple locations of an organization over a shared internet service provider network while keeping the traffic logically separate and private. The VPN routes traffic based on IP addresses (Layer 3), not at a lower hardware level. A service provider builds and operates the infrastructure; a customer controls what locations connect and what routes their traffic takes.

Both the customer and the service provider need management systems to keep the VPN running reliably. The customer must provision sites, configure routing, monitor service levels, and track costs. The provider must maintain the underlying network resources, diagnose faults, ensure security, and provision each customer's logical services. These two viewpoints—service management from the customer's perspective and network management from the provider's side—require different information models and functions.
sections.plainLanguage: An L3VPN is like a private postal service running through a public highway system. The customer decides which addresses connect and how to route their mail. The provider maintains the roads and sorting centers and makes sure customer mail stays separate from others.

sections.title: Two Layers of Management
sections.content:
The framework divides management into two parts. Customer Service Management sits at the top, where a service manager administrates customer-specific attributes: contact information, billing, IP address assignments, routing parameters, and encryption keys if needed. The customer receives a view of their service: what sites connect, whether the agreed service level is being met, and how to request changes.

Provider Network Management sits below, where a network manager oversees the physical and logical infrastructure that realizes the customer service. This includes physical links, router configurations, security services, QoS parameters, and the integration of multiple customer VPNs on shared equipment. The two layers must coordinate: when a customer orders a new site, the provider network management must provision the underlying resources and confirm that the service level can be met.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a restaurant franchise. The customer (restaurant owner) talks to a manager about which dishes to offer and how many customers they expect. Below, the supply chain management team coordinates ingredients, kitchens, and delivery so the promised menu actually works.

sections.title: What Customers Need to Manage
sections.content:
From the customer's perspective, management involves five traditional functions used across telecommunications: fault management, configuration management, accounting, performance management, and security management (known as FCAPS). Customers need to know which of their services are working, request changes to the configuration, receive usage reports, check that they are getting the quality they paid for, and be confident their traffic is secure.

Customers must be able to order new VPN services by selecting from templates (for example, an IPsec-based template or a BGP/MPLS template with specified QoS levels). They must monitor whether the service is up, receive probes to test connectivity, understand why a service failed, and receive monthly measurements showing what fraction of time the service was available. They should also receive responses when they make dynamic requests to change parameters within the bounds of their service agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers want five things: to know when something breaks, to set up new connections, to see how much they used, to verify they got good speed, and to keep their traffic private. All of this should work through a simple interface, not by calling the provider every time.

sections.title: What Providers Must Manage
sections.content:
From the provider's perspective, management covers the same five FCAPS functions but focused on the infrastructure. Providers must detect faults in physical equipment and the network, isolate which customers are affected, and initiate repairs. They must provision PE (Provider Edge) routers, CE (Customer Edge) devices, tunnels, access connections, routing protocols, and QoS parameters. They track resource utilization and perform accounting so they can bill customers accurately and plan capacity.

Providers also must monitor performance: measuring QoS metrics like latency and packet loss, checking for congestion, and alerting when a customer's service level is degraded. When the RFC was written, proprietary command-line interfaces were common, forcing operators to learn multiple vendor languages. The framework recommends that solutions support standard management protocols (particularly SNMP) and automated provisioning to reduce costs and errors, especially as networks grow and vendors multiply.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers handle the heavy lifting: watching thousands of connections, fixing broken links, assigning network capacity to each customer, tracking usage, spotting problems before they get bad, and keeping all customer traffic safely separated.

sections.title: Reference Models and Device Management
sections.content:
The framework presents two architectures based on where VPN logic lives. In PE-based L3VPNs, the provider's edge router handles all VPN routing and configuration. In CE-based L3VPNs, the customer's equipment participates more actively. The framework also structures management into three layers: service management (customer-facing), network management (provider's resource orchestration), and network element management (managing individual devices like routers). These layers must communicate: the service manager initiates a request, the network manager translates it into device configurations, and network element management configures each device accordingly.

Each L3VPN solution must define an information model that specifies what data needs to be managed. This can be a Management Information Base (MIB) for SNMP, a Policy Information Base (PIB), or XML schemas. Standard interfaces allow different vendors' equipment to coexist and allow customers to self-manage their devices with provider oversight. The framework stresses that manual provisioning does not scale; automated provisioning via standard protocols is essential for modern VPN deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider builds a management hierarchy: a service layer that talks to customers, a network layer that figures out what to do, and a device layer that executes those plans. Each level speaks a different language; information models are the dictionary so everything understands what the others mean.
